evidence_note: Web sources were opened or re-opened in the retrieval batch; access_utc records batch start, not a provider crawl time. Full text was not available for S17 and S18 in this session, so only their surfaced publisher-abstract evidence is recorded.
source_ids: Stable IDs are assigned once and must not be silently rebound.

sources.title: Guttation: A Pressure Relief for Plants
sources.source_type: University of Missouri Integrated Pest Management extension article
sources.version_release_commit: Published 2009-06-01; no later revision shown.
sources.locator: Night-condition/hydathode discussion; rendered lines 35–52.
sources.observed_operation: Describes guttation as liquid water exuded from hydathodes at leaf margins/tips when transpiration is low and root pressure moves water under high humidity, cool air, and warm soil. Notes that droplets can resemble dew.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: A margin/tip pattern is consistent with guttation but not conclusive. The article notes rare bacterial entry via droplets and possible edema association under prolonged humidity/excess moisture; neither is evidenced here.
sources.applicability: Mechanism only. Species is unknown; morphology and frequency cannot identify the droplets. Compare air/leaf dew-point conditions, irrigation timing/splash, and plant records.

sources.title: Controlling the Greenhouse Environment
sources.source_type: University of Alaska Fairbanks Cooperative Extension publication HGA-00336
sources.version_release_commit: PDF filename carries 2024-11-27; document HGA-00336.
sources.locator: Printed pp. 9–11, Air Circulation, Humidity Control, and Ventilation and Airflow; rendered lines 601–697.
sources.observed_operation: Explains mixing, dew-point condensation, and canopy variation; distinguishes internal horizontal airflow (HAF) from air exchange. HAF mixes local air; ventilation removes moist air.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: HAF is not a substitute for air exchange; airflow must cross/penetrate canopy and fan operation should coordinate with exhaust. Numerical sizing and Alaska season context are not universal setpoints.
sources.applicability: Identify the changed fan's actual function and map microclimate. Sizing advice is not directly transferable without greenhouse, climate, crop, and system details.

sources.title: Greenhouse Ventilation
sources.source_type: UF/IFAS Extension engineering publication AE-10
sources.version_release_commit: DOI 10.32473/edis-ae030-2019; edition AE-10 (2019 DOI edition).
sources.locator: PDF pp. 1–3, winter ventilation, condensation, and summer ventilation; rendered lines 0–108.
sources.observed_operation: Defines ventilation as removing indoor air and replacing it with outside air. Explains condensation when a surface is below air dew point and that ventilation may reduce humidity but raise winter heat demand.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: Worked rates depend on stated greenhouse, weather, and crop assumptions. Excess ventilation raises heat demand and very low RH may affect growth.
sources.applicability: Separates circulation from exhaust and cautions against prescribing a fan schedule without weather, system, crop, and heating context.

sources.title: Guidelines for measuring and reporting environmental parameters for experiments in greenhouses
sources.source_type: Peer-reviewed Plant Methods commentary by Both et al.
sources.version_release_commit: Version of record, Plant Methods 11:43, published 2015-09-11; DOI 10.1186/s13007-015-0083-5.
sources.locator: PDF pp. 6–8 and Table 2: sensor placement, calibration, temperature, atmospheric moisture and substrate water; rendered lines 397–439.
sources.observed_operation: Recommends measurements in multiple feasible locations and as frequently as practical, with location, shielding/aspiration, summary statistics and calibration recorded. Recommends canopy-level measurements independent of the greenhouse control sensor.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: Guidance is for replicable greenhouse experiments; effort and variables should match the study, not serve as crop-specific operating standards.
sources.applicability: Supports a mapped baseline with disclosed sensor position and calibration rather than reliance on one control sensor.

sources.title: Measuring the Sprinkler Irrigation Requirement of Container-Grown Nursery Plants
sources.source_type: UF/IFAS Extension publication ENH1197/EP458
sources.version_release_commit: Publication identifier ENH1197/EP458; retrieved page did not expose a publication/revision date.
sources.locator: Three factors determining irrigation requirement; container ET and weighing procedure; lines 17–36 and 62–64.
sources.observed_operation: Frames container irrigation as evapotranspiration plus plant/canopy capture and distribution uniformity. Describes weighing representative containers before and after a day to estimate water loss.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: Guide is for container nurseries with sprinklers; plant size, container, spacing, weather and canopy affect results. Its example values are not herb targets.
sources.applicability: Use concepts to reconstruct water delivery and compare representative pots; do not apply nursery rates or infer deficit from symptoms.

sources.title: Field Evaluation of Container Nursery Irrigation Systems: Measuring Uniformity of Water Application of Sprinkler Systems
sources.source_type: UF/IFAS Extension publication FS98-2/AE194
sources.version_release_commit: Original 2001; revised 2022-07-26; reviewed 2025-08-12; DOI 10.32473/edis-ae194-2001.
sources.locator: Causes of low uniformity and catch-can lower-quarter method; lines 18–40.
sources.observed_operation: Identifies pressure, pipe/nozzle selection, overlap, wind, aging components, and clogging as sources of uneven output; outlines a mapped catch-can test and notes uniformity changes over time.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: For overhead sprinkler zones; catch cans run during a defined event. It does not measure substrate moisture or root uptake.
sources.applicability: If overhead delivery is used, a mapped output test can assess position differences without changing crop settings. For drip, measure emitter output and pressure.

sources.title: Irrigation System Check-ups
sources.source_type: University of Maryland Extension greenhouse/nursery guidance
sources.version_release_commit: Retrieved page exposes no publication/revision date; current page version as accessed.
sources.locator: Watering using an irrigation system and Uniformity Test; lines 55–74.
sources.observed_operation: Recommends checking that pots are wetted through, inspecting pressure and clogged/worn emitters, and mapping catch containers to identify uneven application.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: Examples cover container crops and blocks; stated thresholds are guidance, not universal herb criteria.
sources.applicability: Supports a low-cost delivery audit once the method is known; not a treatment recommendation.

sources.title: The Use of Soil Moisture Probes for Improved Uniformity and Irrigation Control in Greenhouses
sources.source_type: International Society for Horticultural Science conference proceeding by van Iersel, Dove, and Burnett
sources.version_release_commit: Acta Horticulturae 893, article 893_119, pp. 1049–1056; DOI version 2011.
sources.locator: Abstract and sensor placement for small versus large containers; ISHS article page lines 78–100.
sources.observed_operation: Explains substrate sensors can support irrigation control; within-pot water distribution, root uptake and sensor characteristics affect the best placement.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: General method discussion, not validation of an unspecified sensor or substrate. A single sensor may represent a small container only under suitable conditions.
sources.applicability: Check sensors against pot-weight/substrate observations in the actual mix and locate in active roots; do not treat uncalibrated values as ground truth.

sources.title: Implementation of Sensor-based Automated Irrigation in Commercial Floriculture Production: A Case Study
sources.source_type: Peer-reviewed HortTechnology commercial greenhouse case study by Wheeler et al.
sources.version_release_commit: HortTechnology 28(6), pp. 719–727, December 2018; DOI 10.21273/HORTTECH04114-18.
sources.locator: Abstract and water-use/setpoint/staff-operation discussion; PDF pp. 1 and 4–6.
sources.observed_operation: Two years of side-by-side poinsettia/geranium trials found no irrigation-water reduction in this grower-controlled sensor setting. The discussion links this partly to repeated upward setpoint changes reflecting historical timer-based habits despite training.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: Commercial poinsettia and geranium, not culinary herbs. System, substrate, season, staff and crop targets differ; labor changed and crop-specific growth differences were also reported.
sources.applicability: Operator behavior can alter results. Recover who changed the timer/fan, why, exact settings and access/override history; a new system alone does not guarantee intended response.

sources.title: Implementation of Soil Moisture Sensor Based Automated Irrigation in Woody Ornamental Production
sources.source_type: Peer-reviewed Journal of Environmental Horticulture commercial nursery case study by Wheeler et al.
sources.version_release_commit: Journal of Environmental Horticulture 38(1), pp. 1–7, March 2020; DOI 10.24266/0738-2898-38.1.1.
sources.locator: Abstract and discussion of crop grouping, overhead capture, salt buildup and staff access; PDF pp. 1 and 4–6.
sources.observed_operation: A 2014–2015 trial reported about 50% less irrigation overall; several woody crops had similar growth/losses, while >50% Rhododendron loss occurred in 2015. Authors associated the exception with cross-species averaged thresholds, canopy water capture, a hot/dry season, and implementation responsibility; more precise irrigation also allowed salts to build up relative to earlier saturating events.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: Woody plants, bark media, overhead capture, and nursery production differ materially from herbs. Proposed causal explanations are not universal thresholds.
sources.applicability: Do not pool crop ages/species/substrates or transfer a water-saving result. Record crop identity, canopy, pot, delivery, season, water and operator history.

sources.title: Subirrigation for Greenhouse Crops
sources.source_type: UMass Extension Greenhouse & Floriculture fact sheet
sources.version_release_commit: No publication/update date visible; date unknown.
sources.locator: Advantages, challenges, and ebb-and-flow sections; retrieved page lines 26 onward.
sources.observed_operation: Describes closed recirculating subirrigation as potentially reducing foliar wetting, labor, water, and nutrient runoff, while requiring investment, retrofit, pH/EC monitoring, cleanliness and recirculated-water management. Different pot sizes may not share an irrigation zone.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: Benefits assume a maintained closed system and compatible crop/container/zone; mats may not be closed. Salt accumulation and sanitation are exceptions.
sources.applicability: A longer-term non-chemical alternative if overhead wetting is verified, not a quick fix for unknown herbs and media.

sources.title: Root Diseases of Greenhouse Crops
sources.source_type: UMass Extension Greenhouse Crops & Floriculture fact sheet
sources.version_release_commit: Updated by Angela Madeiras; last updated 2019-10-03.
sources.locator: Introduction, abiotic causes, root examination, and source pathways; lines 19–46.
sources.observed_operation: Separates abiotic root impairment (salts, ammonium toxicity, saturated/oxygen-poor media) from pathogen causes; notes above-ground symptoms overlap and accurate diagnosis is needed.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: Only diagnostic-limit content is used; treatment material is outside the assignment boundary.
sources.applicability: Supports specialist escalation for root/crown concerns. Cannot diagnose this case or justify fertilizer/pesticide action.

sources.title: Diagnostics System for Crop History and Disorders in Greenhouses and Nurseries
sources.source_type: University of Georgia Extension Bulletin 1273 by Pennisi and Thomas
sources.version_release_commit: Bulletin 1273 published with full review 2022-07-25.
sources.locator: Diagnostic forms and sections for environment, crop, symptoms, testing; page lines 197–231 and 266–279.
sources.observed_operation: Promotes documented crop history and diagnostic workflow, assignment of record/follow-up responsibility, examination below ground when aerial clues are insufficient, and calibrated night temperature records.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: Written for production operations and more formal than a small teaching bench may need; it is a recordkeeping model, not a diagnosis.
sources.applicability: Use as a structure for who/what/when history, map, symptom records and referral.

sources.title: Diagnosing Horticultural Plant Problems
sources.source_type: University of Delaware Cooperative Extension fact sheet
sources.version_release_commit: Reviewed March 2025.
sources.locator: Diagnostic principles and sample submission guidance; lines 230–231 and symptom/sign key.
sources.observed_operation: Emphasizes multiple causes for symptoms, patterns as clues rather than diagnosis, and that some cases need representative sampling, clinic submission, incubation, or further testing.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: General horticultural guidance; clinic requirements differ by suspected problem.
sources.applicability: Escalate for progression, unclear signs, or decisions needing confirmation; provide history and representative sample via a diagnostic service.

sources.title: Pest Management for Herb Bedding Plants Grown in the Greenhouse
sources.source_type: University of Connecticut IPM Extension reference
sources.version_release_commit: Retrieved page does not show a publication/revision date.
sources.locator: Disease, environment, and humidity sections; lines 525–538 and herb examples.
sources.observed_operation: Warns that environmental/nutritional/salt/planting-depth disorders can mimic infectious disease in herbs. Discusses airflow and heat/vent mechanisms and diagnostic confirmation.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: Herb bedding production is relevant, but practices vary by herb, season, and greenhouse; not an instruction to intervene here.
sources.applicability: Species identity and specialist diagnosis matter; environmental mechanisms are hypotheses, not fixed fan or irrigation settings.

sources.title: Basil downy mildew
sources.source_type: University of Minnesota Extension crop disease reference
sources.version_release_commit: Retrieved current page; no date/revision shown.
sources.locator: Symptom key, biology and cultural controls; lines 241–276.
sources.observed_operation: If crop is basil, this source describes lower-leaf yellowing constrained by major veins and gray growth on undersides as a distinct pattern, and discusses moisture/airflow context.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: Only applies if species is basil and a diagnosis is confirmed; local climate/pathogen occurrence matter. Case lacks species and distinguishing signs.
sources.applicability: Conditional referral cue only. Do not identify this disease from pale lower leaves or droplets.

sources.title: A Wetness Sensor for Detecting Condensation on Tomato Plants in Greenhouses
sources.source_type: Peer-reviewed Journal of Agricultural Engineering Research study by Wei, Bailey, and Stenning
sources.version_release_commit: Volume 61, issue 3, July 1995, pp. 197–204; DOI version.
sources.locator: Publisher abstract: sensor build/test and comparison with fruit-surface/dew-point temperature.
sources.observed_operation: Abstract reports uncoated sensors responded repeatably to condensation; coatings absorbed/released moisture slowly and overestimated wetness duration. Sensor wetness aligned with surface/dew-point comparison under tested tomato conditions.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: 1995 tomato sensor design, not a modern specification or validation on unknown herb leaves. Direct publisher fetch errored; evidence is abstract-level only.
sources.applicability: If using a leaf-wetness logger, validate that model/crop surface; it cannot distinguish dew, guttation or irrigation splash by itself.

sources.title: Development of a method for condensation rate measurement on flat surfaces
sources.source_type: Peer-reviewed Information Processing in Agriculture study by Han and Guo
sources.version_release_commit: Information Processing in Agriculture 5(4), December 2018, pp. 490–497; DOI version.
sources.locator: Publisher abstract on chamber calibration of a commercial leaf-wetness sensor for known condensate on a flat surface.
sources.observed_operation: Reports chamber calibration across controlled temperatures/RH with known sprayed water mass; output was linearly related to condensate on the test sensor surface.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: Tested condensation on a flat sensor in a chamber, not biological leaf behavior or diagnosis. Full publisher fetch failed, so evidence is abstract-level.
sources.applicability: Specialized candidate only if wetness amount is important and can be validated; cannot infer droplet source.

sources.title: Temperature and Humidity Gradients in Fan Ventilated Greenhouses under Two Cooling Modes
sources.source_type: ISHS Acta Horticulturae peer-reviewed proceeding by Teitel, Barak, and Zhao
sources.version_release_commit: Acta Horticulturae 614, article 614_70; DOI version 2003.
sources.locator: Abstract lines 16–25; pepper crop in a fan-only versus fan-and-pad greenhouse, with two ventilation rates.
sources.observed_operation: Reports measured temperature/humidity gradients along the greenhouse and with height; gradient patterns and ventilation-rate effects differed by cooling mode. In both modes, humidity conditions differed from ambient.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: Warm-climate greenhouse with tall pepper crop and fan/pad equipment; mode-specific observations cannot be treated as effect sizes for a teaching herb bench.
sources.applicability: Supports mapping multiple positions and identifying actual fan/vent configuration before making a climate claim.

sources.title: Wireless sensor network to map the meteorological variability in a greenhouse with evaporative cooling
sources.source_type: ISHS Acta Horticulturae proceeding by Zorzeto and Leal
sources.version_release_commit: Acta Horticulturae 1154, article 1154_28; DOI version 2017.
sources.locator: Abstract lines 16–24; sensor network, horizontal/vertical variability and evaporative cooling/shading conditions.
sources.observed_operation: Mapped temperature/RH heterogeneity in a Brazilian greenhouse using evaporative cooling; patterns varied between fan/pad and window/vent configurations and across horizontal/vertical positions.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: São Paulo greenhouse with evaporative cooling and fixed shade; reported magnitudes are not transferable to an unidentified teaching greenhouse.
sources.applicability: Primary implementation evidence for mapping rather than assuming the door or one control sensor represents the bench.

sources.title: Measuring Nursery Plant Water Use in Containers
sources.source_type: Virginia Tech/Virginia Cooperative Extension expert-reviewed publication SPES-750P by Kristopher Criscione
sources.version_release_commit: Publication date 2026-01-13; SPES-750P.
sources.locator: Factors affecting ET, container weighing protocol, and drip emitter beaker measurement; rendered lines 141–190.
sources.observed_operation: Describes container water loss as evaporation plus transpiration, varying with crop/canopy, growth stage, weather, substrate, container and cultural practice; gives a weigh-after-drain then 24-hour reweigh method and emitter flow check.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: Outdoor nursery plant guidance and its optional instruction to wait until wilting is not suitable as a protocol for this assignment; no intentional stress is proposed.
sources.applicability: Supports weighing representative pots and measuring emitter output, while explicitly accounting for age, substrate and weather; do not apply its nursery rates or induce wilting.
